newsitem.title: USA: Confirmation hearing set for U.S. Vietnam envoy.
newsitem.headline: Confirmation hearing set for U.S. Vietnam envoy.

text.p: Senate confirmation hearings for President Bill Clinton's nominee to be the first U.S. ambassador to Vietnam will begin next Thursday despite a last-ditch effort by key House Republicans to delay them, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said on Thursday.
Clinton's nominee is former Representative Pete Peterson, a retired Air Force fighter pilot held as a prisoner of war for six-and-a-half years after his aircraft was shot down near Hanoi in 1966.
If confirmed as expected, Peterson, who served in House as a Florida Democrat from 1991 until last year, would become the first U.S. ambassador in Hanoi.
Previous U.S. ambassadors were accredited to the U.S.-backed South Vietnamese government in Saigon that was overrun by the Communist-ruled North in April 1975.
After years of friction over the more than 2,000 U.S. servicemen listed as missing from the war, President Bill Clinton established diplomatic relations with Vietnam in July 1995.

But unanswered questions about the fate of some of those men have kept relations on a slow track, with normal trade status yet to be worked out. The appointment of an ambassador probably would give a new shot in the arm to economic normalisation, U.S. officials have said. The U.S. embassy in Hanoi is currently headed by Desaix Anderson, a career foreign service with the title of charge d'affaires.

The chairman of the House Committee on International Relations and three colleagues had urged in a letter on Wednesday that confirmation hearings be postponed until completion of congressional probes into whether U.S. policy toward Vietnam had been improperly influenced by illegal foreign financial contributions to President Clinton's re-election effort.

A spokesman for Senator Jesse Helms, the North Carolina Republican who chairs the Foreign Relations Committee, did not immediately return a phone call seeking comment on the decision to go ahead with the hearing despite the request from his House counterpart, Ben Gilman of New York.

In their letters to Helms and to Craig Thomas, the Wyoming Republican who heads the subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific, Gilman and his colleagues said it was "imperative for Congress and the American people to know whether or not U.S. foreign policy toward Vietnam is wholly, or in part, the result of illegal foreign financial contributions."

"We strongly believe it would be irresponsible for the Senate to now begin action, at the president's request, to confirm an ambassador to Vietnam," added the letter, which was also signed by Gerald Solomon of New York, chairman of the House Rules Committee; Dan Burton of Indiana, chair of the Committee on Government Reform; and Sam Johnson of Texas, a member of the U.S.-Russian Joint Commission on POW/MIAs (prisoners of war/missing in action).
